European robins (Erithacus rubecula) begin their development within a calcareous egg incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], and the incubation period concludes with hatching after approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days]. At the moment of emergence, the altricial nestling weighs only 2.4 grams [Ww0 = 2.4 grams], a value that represents the initial wet weight of the newly hatched chick before exogenous feeding begins. This modest neonatal mass, measured shortly after the egg tooth penetrates the shell, is typical of small passerines and reflects the substantial energetic investment still required from the provisioning adults. The nestling period is characterized by rapid mass gain driven by intensive parental feeding, and the chick remains entirely dependent on its parents for both warmth and food during this vulnerable phase. This early developmental phase is critical for establishing the physiological foundation for subsequent growth, with the altricial chick undergoing a series of morphological and behavioral changes that prepare it for the demands of independent life outside the nest cavity.

Field studies have documented that newly hatched chicks exhibit a wet weight at birth of approximately 1.8 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.8 grams], a figure that represents the body mass recorded immediately following the completion of hatching. This value is slightly lower than the initial wet weight measured shortly before hatching, likely due to the substantial metabolic costs associated with the hatching process itself. Under the typical thermal conditions of an actively brooding adult, which maintains a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the developmental trajectory proceeds through clearly defined milestones. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest, occurs at 14 days after hatching [tx = 14 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively short nestling period is characteristic of many temperate-zone passerines and appears to be an adaptive response to reduce predation risk during the stationary phase of development. The timing of fledging is influenced by both environmental conditions and the quality of parental provisioning, with broods in resource-rich territories often achieving independence slightly earlier than those in marginal habitats.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult European robins is 18.6 grams [Wwi = 18.6 grams], a value that represents the asymptotic body mass of a fully grown, reproductively active individual. This adult mass is achieved following a period of rapid somatic growth that continues beyond the fledging stage into the post-dispersal juvenile phase. When the metabolic conditions associated with active foraging and territorial defense prevail (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), the timing of subsequent life-history events follows a predictable schedule. Sexual maturation, marked by the onset of gonadal activity and the development of functional reproductive organs, is attained at 42 days after hatching [tp = 42 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively rapid attainment of puberty, occurring roughly six weeks post-hatching, is consistent with the species' life-history strategy as a short-lived, iteroparous passerine that must begin breeding early in its first calendar year. The rapid onset of reproductive capability is facilitated by the species' ability to exploit abundant invertebrate prey during the late spring and summer months.

Under the same thermal regime characteristic of active metabolism (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), the age at which female European robins produce their first brood has been documented at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching]. This one-year delay between the attainment of sexual maturity and first reproduction is ecologically significant, as it allows young birds to acquire a high-quality territory and accumulate sufficient body condition before initiating reproductive effort. Reproductive output is characterized by a clutch size of approximately 5.17 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 5.17 eggs per clutch], with females typically producing 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = 2 clutches per year], yielding a maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 0.0284 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 0.0284 eggs per day] under these conditions. This two-clutch annual schedule is common among temperate-zone passerines and allows the species to capitalize on the extended breeding season available in European woodlands, with the first clutch often initiated in late March and the second following in June or July.

Maximum longevity in European robins has been recorded at 19.3 years [am = 19.3 years], a figure drawn from extensive ringing studies and representing the time elapsed since birth at the oldest confirmed individual at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This lifespan was documented in a wild bird under natural thermal conditions at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], and it substantially exceeds the average expectation for a passerine of this body size, particularly among temperate-region species. The species' capacity for extended survival is partly attributable to its partial migratory behavior, with many populations remaining resident in mild European climates throughout the winter, thereby avoiding the substantial mortality risks associated with long-distance migration. The ability to maintain a stable body temperature through endogenous thermogenesis, even at the relatively high metabolic set point of 41.6 °C, is energetically costly but allows sustained activity during cold periods when food availability may be unpredictable, contributing to the species' notable longevity among small passerines.
